extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and practitioners in autoformalization, formal theorem proving, and machine learning for mathematics (users of Lean/mathlib and ML-based theorem proving systems).
extracted.subtask_description: A benchmark (ProofNet) of parallel natural-language and Lean 3 formal theorem statements (and some informal proofs) drawn from undergraduate pure-mathematics textbook exercises, intended to evaluate autoformalization and formal/informal theorem-proving systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-containment
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems should only depend on the results commonly taught in an undergraduate curriculum. In particular, this rules out problems that are split into multiple sequentially dependent parts, or those using nonstandard notations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select exercises that can be understood and formalized without needing earlier parts of a multipart exercise or specialized notation. Exclude sequentially dependent multi-part problems and exercises that rely on nonstandard symbols or conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of formalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all kinds of mathematical problems can be naturally formalized, such as word problems, and such problems are excluded. We do not include exercises that require computing an unknown quantity. We do not include problems that depend on parts of Lean’s mathlib that are relatively less mature, such as Euclidean geometry or combinatorics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer problems that map naturally to Lean/mathlib concepts (statements about definitions, lemmas, concrete applications). Exclude: word problems, numeric computation problems (solving for unknowns), and problems that would require immature or thin mathlib support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low risk of train-test overlap
rubrics_metrics.description: Because language models are often pre-trained on large corpora mined from the internet that include mathlib, we refrain from including statements that are in mathlib or are likely to be added to mathlib in the future. In practice, this means we avoid the abstract 'theory-building' style of theorems that constitute mathlib, and instead choose problems that involve applying general results to specific cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including statements verbatim present in mathlib or of the same abstract, generalizing style. Prefer concrete-instance problems less likely to appear in pretraining corpora or later be added to mathlib to reduce memorization/test contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad curriculum coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the above criteria, problems were selected for broad coverage of the undergraduate curriculum and to range in difficulty from straightforward applications of the definitions to those requiring ingenious creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include problems across analysis, complex analysis, linear algebra, abstract algebra, topology, etc., so the benchmark exercises reasoning over the typical core undergraduate topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems range in difficulty from straightforward applications of the definitions to those requiring ingenious creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the dataset to include a spectrum of challenge levels so models are tested on both routine formalizations and more inventive/creative statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcription and formalization quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem statements are transcribed into LATEX and formalized by human annotators proficient in Lean. Natural language (informal) proofs are adapted from online solutions manuals, or in a few cases, written by the annotators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use skilled human annotators to produce high-quality LaTeX transcriptions and idiomatic Lean formal statements; adapt informal proofs from authoritative solutions or write them carefully when needed to ensure alignment with formal versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supported evaluation tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: ProofNet supports the following distinct tasks: formal theorem proving (given a formal statement, produce a formal proof); informal theorem proving (given an informal statement, produce an informal proof); formalization and informalization of statements (translate between informal and formal statement forms); formalization of proofs (given informal statement + informal proof + formal statement, produce a formal proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each supported task as a separate evaluation target; dataset provides parallel artifacts (informal statements, informal proofs, formal statements) enabling these distinct tasks and their combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human expert correctness evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because there are often many idiomatic ways of formalizing a given natural language theorem, all autoformalizations are evaluated for correctness by a human expert. Informalizations are also evaluated by a human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on automated syntactic checks; use human reviewers familiar with Lean/mathlib to judge whether generated formalizations capture the intended meaning (semantic correctness) even when multiple idiomatic formulations exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typecheck rate (evaluation metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typecheck rate: the proportion of a model’s samples that are accepted by Lean’s type system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report this metric to capture whether generated Lean code is well-typed; note that typechecking is necessary but not sufficient for semantic correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (evaluation metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy: proportion of generated outputs judged correct (for formalization/informalization tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by human evaluation for formalization/informalization tasks. For formalization, accuracy reflects correct semantic translation to Lean; for informalization, accuracy reflects natural-language fidelity and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile rate (evaluation metric for informalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile rate: proportion of the model’s informalization samples that produce LaTeX which compiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for informalization task to ensure generated natural-language/LaTeX output is syntactically valid; failures commonly due to Unicode or symbols not accepted by pdflatex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope: proofs left for future work
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the technical challenges involved in building interactive proving environments in Lean, we leave the investigation of autoformalizing proofs and formally proving ProofNet problems to future work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current benchmark primarily targets statement formalization/informalization and (separately) formal theorem proving when a formal statement is given; full autoformalization of informal proofs to formal proofs was deferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic selection guideline (mathlib vs ProofNet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathlib emphasizes including the most abstract and general formulations of mathematical results, whereas ProofNet predominantly tests the ability of models to apply those results in concrete instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete-instance problems over abstract theory-building statements; this stylistic choice reduces overlap with mathlib and exercises models' ability to apply general theorems to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalization correctness desiderata (lexical, idiomatic, logical, type requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct and idiomatic Lean/mathlib formalization requires proper lexical choices (correct identifiers/typeclasses), idiomatic usage of mathlib conventions (e.g., ideal R, is_maximal predicate, coercions to sets), and logically appropriate hypotheses (e.g., declaring inner_product_space and is_R_or_C when orthogonal complements are used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful formalization must: (1) use the right mathlib names and typeclasses, (2) include all implicit hypotheses needed for constructs to make sense (e.g., inner product structure and field restrictions), (3) respect coercions and notation expected by mathlib, and (4) typecheck under Lean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typecheck ≠ semantic correctness (evaluation nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among Code-davinci-002’s generations that type-check, roughly half are correct formalizations. This is consistent with the hypothesis that the model performs well in the cases where it is able to generate valid Lean code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate syntactic/type correctness with full semantic/ logical correctness; report both typecheck rate and human-judged accuracy and analyze failure modes (lexical mistakes, missing hypotheses, logical errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline methodology: few-shot prompting
rubrics_metrics.description: Few-shot learning with a manually constructed prompt is used as the baseline for autoformalizing and informalizing theorem statements; prompts include multiple translation examples and are adjusted for model context length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide 6–12 high-quality natural/formal translation pairs as few-shot examples, adapt number based on model context window, and evaluate generations with the metrics above. When evaluating, account for model context-size differences (e.g., GPT-J vs Code-davinci-002).
